cues.text:
How could a clock tell sailors
where they were in the ocean?

In the 1700s, ships far from land
struggled to work out
how far east or west they had sailed.

When the sun reached its highest point,
sailors knew it was noon on the ship.

If a clock still showed the time back home,
they could compare the two
and calculate their position east or west.

But a clock had to stay accurate
through a long, rolling voyage.

English clockmaker John Harrison
spent years working on one that could.

In 1761, his son took Harrison's watch,
known as H4, on a voyage to Jamaica.

It kept time accurately enough to prove
that the method could work at sea.

The ship could use the time back home
to help find its place on the ocean.
